Clinical Reference

Supraventricular Tachycardia

On this page
A regular, abrupt-onset tachycardia of 150–250 bpm arising at or above the bundle of His — most often a re-entry circuit that uses the AV node as one of its limbs, which is exactly why blocking the node stops it.
Prevalence 2.25/1000 · incidence 35/100,000 person-yrs AVNRT ~60% · AVRT ~30% · atrial tach ~10% Adenosine 6 → 12 → 18 mg rapid IV push Irregular + wide = pre-excited AF → NO AV-nodal blockers Ablation cures it: AVNRT 97%, AVRT 92%
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

"Supraventricular tachycardia" is an anatomic statement, not a single disease: the rhythm originates at or above the bundle of His, so it uses the normal His–Purkinje system to reach the ventricles and the QRS stays narrow (<120 ms) unless something else widens it. In everyday usage — and in this guide — "SVT" means the paroxysmal, regular, narrow-complex tachycardias: AVNRT, AVRT, and focal atrial tachycardia. Atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter are technically supraventricular too, but they behave and are treated so differently that they get their own guides.

Three electrophysiologic mechanisms can produce a tachycardia, and knowing which one you are facing tells you what will work:

  • Re-entry (the overwhelming majority, ~90%) — a circular circuit of tissue in which the impulse chases its own tail. Requires two limbs with different conduction speeds and different refractory periods, plus a trigger (a premature beat) that arrives when one limb is still refractory. Because the circuit is a fixed loop, the rate is metronome-regular and it starts and stops instantly — the classic "light-switch" history.
  • Enhanced automaticity — an ectopic focus depolarizes spontaneously faster than the sinus node. It warms up at onset and cools down at offset, is often catecholamine-sensitive, and cannot be terminated by blocking the AV node (focal atrial tachycardia, multifocal atrial tachycardia, junctional ectopic tachycardia).
  • Triggered activity — afterdepolarizations riding on the preceding action potential, classically from digoxin toxicity, hypokalemia, or high catecholamine states (some focal ATs).
Re-entry is a roundabout with a fast lane and a slow lane. Normally a car (the impulse) enters, goes both ways around, the two halves crash head-on, and everything stops — that's a normal sinus beat. Now imagine the fast lane is briefly closed for maintenance (still refractory after the last beat). An early car is forced into the slow lane. It crawls around, and by the time it reaches the far side the fast lane has re-opened — so instead of crashing, it turns up the fast lane, comes back to the entrance, and finds the slow lane ready again. Now it's circling the roundabout forever at 200 laps per minute, throwing off a car toward the ventricles on every lap. Adenosine, vagal maneuvers, and calcium channel blockers all work by closing one lane of the roundabout for a couple of seconds. The car has nowhere to go, the circuit collapses, and sinus rhythm resumes. Ablation is the permanent fix — it bulldozes one lane so the roundabout can never form again.
From premature beat to sustained circuit — and the exact point at which each therapy interrupts it. Green boxes are the interventions; note that focal atrial tachycardia sits outside the AV-node-dependent loop, which is why adenosine unmasks it rather than curing it.
The normal conduction system. The AV node is the only electrical connection between atria and ventricles — a deliberate bottleneck. In AVNRT the circuit lives inside that bottleneck; in AVRT an extra strand of muscle bypasses it entirely.
Madhero88 · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Conductionsystemoftheheart.png
Wolff–Parkinson–White: an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) carries the impulse straight from atrium to ventricle, skipping the AV node's built-in delay. That early, slow, muscle-to-muscle activation is the delta wave.
CardioNetworks: Drj · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Wpw2 (CardioNetworks ECGpedia).svg

The three circuits you must be able to draw

1. AVNRT — atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia (~60% of SVT)

About 25% of people have dual AV nodal physiology: the AV node is functionally split into a fast pathway (conducts quickly but has a long refractory period) and a slow pathway (conducts slowly but recovers quickly). Most never know it. When a premature atrial beat arrives while the fast pathway is still refractory, it is forced down the slow pathway; the delay is long enough that the fast pathway recovers, so the impulse turns around and travels retrograde up the fast pathway — and the loop is closed. This is typical ("slow–fast") AVNRT, ~90% of AVNRT.

Because retrograde atrial activation up the fast pathway is nearly simultaneous with ventricular activation, the P wave is buried in the QRS or peeks out at its very end: a pseudo-R′ in V1 and a pseudo-S in the inferior leads that were not there in sinus rhythm. Atypical ("fast–slow") AVNRT runs the loop backwards and produces a long-RP tachycardia with inverted P waves in II, III, aVF — about 6% of AVNRT cases.

2. AVRT — atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia (~30%)

Here the second limb is an accessory pathway: a congenital strand of working myocardium that crosses the AV groove where the fibrous annulus should have insulated atrium from ventricle. The circuit is macro-re-entrant — down one limb, through the ventricle, up the other, through the atrium.

  • Orthodromic AVRT (~95% of AVRT): antegrade down the AV node, retrograde up the accessory pathway. The ventricles are activated normally, so the QRS is narrow. Because retrograde atrial activation must traverse ventricle → pathway → atrium, the P wave falls clearly after the QRS — an RP interval >70–90 ms. Any delta wave that was present in sinus rhythm disappears during the tachycardia.
  • Antidromic AVRT (~5%): antegrade down the accessory pathway, retrograde up the node. The ventricle is depolarized muscle-to-muscle from the pathway insertion — a maximally pre-excited, wide, bizarre QRS that is easily mistaken for VT.

WPW pattern vs WPW syndrome: the ECG pattern is a short PR (<120 ms) + delta wave + wide QRS in sinus rhythm — pre-excitation, present in ~0.15–0.25% of the population. The syndrome is that pattern plus documented arrhythmia. A "concealed" accessory pathway conducts only retrograde, so the resting ECG is completely normal — yet it can still sustain orthodromic AVRT.

3. Focal atrial tachycardia (~10%)

An ectopic atrial focus — commonly at the crista terminalis, tricuspid/mitral annulus, pulmonary vein ostia, or coronary sinus — fires faster than the sinus node by automaticity, micro-re-entry, or triggered activity. The P-wave morphology differs from sinus and the tachycardia is long-RP. Because the AV node is a bystander, not part of the circuit, blocking the node slows the ventricular response and reveals the atrial rhythm but does not terminate it. Incessant focal AT is the classic cause of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy.

Every drug in this guide interrupts one specific step. Adenosine binds the A1 receptor on nodal cells → Gi protein → opens the acetylcholine-sensitive potassium channel (IKAdo/GIRK) and simultaneously inhibits adenylyl cyclase → the cell hyperpolarizes and the L-type calcium current falls → transient complete AV block for a few seconds. Vagal maneuvers reach the same channel through a different door: baroreceptor stretch → efferent vagal acetylcholine → the same GIRK current. Verapamil and diltiazem block the L-type calcium channel that is the AV node's upstroke — nodal tissue is calcium-dependent, not sodium-dependent, which is why non-dihydropyridine CCBs slow the node while amlodipine does nothing. Beta-blockers cut sympathetic cAMP, indirectly reducing both If and ICaL. Flecainide and propafenone block sodium channels in fast-response tissue — atrium, ventricle, and accessory pathways — which is why they are the drugs that target the pathway itself rather than the node. Ablation deletes a limb of the circuit permanently.
Nodal tissue (SA node, AV node) depolarizes with calcium; atrium, ventricle, His–Purkinje and accessory pathways depolarize with sodium. That single fact predicts the entire pharmacology: calcium blockers hit nodes, sodium blockers hit pathways and myocardium, and drugs that do neither (like amlodipine, a vascular dihydropyridine) do nothing to rhythm at all.

Mechanism distribution and epidemiology per the 2019 ESC SVT Guidelines: general-population SVT prevalence 2.25/1000, incidence 35/100,000 person-years, women at 2× the risk of men, and a 5× higher risk in older versus younger adults.

Reading the ECG — the whole diagnosis lives here

📈

Two questions answer almost everything: how wide, and how regular?

Before you reach for a drug, answer two binary questions off the monitor. They sort every tachycardia into four boxes, and the box determines both the differential and the danger.

RegularIrregular
Narrow (<120 ms)Sinus tach · AVNRT · orthodromic AVRT · focal AT · atrial flutter with fixed block · junctional tachAtrial fibrillation · MAT · atrial flutter with variable block
Wide (≥120 ms)VT until proven otherwise · SVT with aberrancy (rate-related or pre-existing BBB) · antidromic AVRT · pacedPRE-EXCITED AF — the one that kills · AF with aberrancy · polymorphic VT/torsades
The bottom-right box is the trap. An irregular, wide, fast (often >200 bpm), beat-to-beat-varying-morphology tachycardia is pre-excited atrial fibrillation until proven otherwise. Giving adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, a beta-blocker, or digoxin here blocks the AV node and forces every atrial impulse down the accessory pathway — which has no decremental conduction — accelerating the ventricular rate into ventricular fibrillation. Treat with IV procainamide or immediate synchronized cardioversion.
Pre-excited AF in WPW. Irregularly irregular, wide, and rapid, with beat-to-beat changing QRS width — impulses reach the ventricle via the accessory pathway (very broad "pure" delta complexes), the AV node (narrow, no delta), or both (fusion). This is the rhythm in which AV-nodal blockers can precipitate VF.
Michael Rosengarten BEng, MD.McGill · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons: E305 (CardioNetworks ECGpedia).jpg
The delta wave in sinus rhythm. Short PR (<120 ms) with a slurred upstroke into the QRS. Pre-excitation is only visible when the atrium is in sinus or fibrillating — it disappears during orthodromic AVRT, because then the pathway is only conducting backwards.
James Heilman, MD · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons: DeltaWave09.JPG

Short RP vs long RP — how to name a regular narrow-complex tachycardia

Find the retrograde P wave, then measure from the start of the QRS to that P (the RP interval) and compare it with the remaining interval to the next QRS (the PR interval). Where the P sits tells you where the circuit is.

Where the retrograde P falls names the circuit. In typical AVNRT the P is so close to the QRS it hides inside it; in orthodromic AVRT the impulse must cross ventricle → pathway → atrium, so the P clears the QRS.
FindingPoints toWhy — the mechanism behind the sign
No visible P at allTypical AVNRTAtria and ventricles depolarize simultaneously; the retrograde P is buried inside the QRS.
Pseudo-R′ in V1 (absent in sinus)Typical AVNRTThe terminal portion of the retrograde P peeking out of the end of the QRS. Comparing to a prior sinus ECG is the trick — the "new" r′ is the P wave.
Pseudo-S in II, III, aVFTypical AVNRTThe same retrograde P, seen from the inferior leads as a negative deflection at the QRS terminus.
RP >70–90 ms, P clearly after QRSOrthodromic AVRTRetrograde conduction has to travel ventricle → accessory pathway → atrium, which takes measurable time.
QRS alternans (alternating amplitude)AVRT (more than AVNRT)Rate-related; classically described with AVRT at high rates. Suggestive, not diagnostic.
Rate very close to 150 bpmAtrial flutter, 2:1Atrial rate ~300 divided by 2. Always look for sawtooth in II/III/aVF and V1 before calling it AVNRT.
P morphology differs from sinus, long RPFocal atrial tachycardiaDepolarization starts somewhere other than the sinus node, so the atrial activation vector — and therefore the P axis — changes.
Gradual warm-up / cool-downFocal AT, sinus tach, ISTAutomatic foci accelerate and decelerate with autonomic tone. Re-entry, by contrast, is on/off like a switch.
≥3 P morphologies + irregularMATMultiple competing atrial foci, each with its own activation vector and its own conduction time to the node.
AV dissociation, capture/fusion beatsVTThe ventricle is driving itself independently of the atria — only possible if the focus is below the His. Highly specific, seen in a minority of VT.
Post-conversion T-wave inversionsBenign "memory" T wavesCardiac memory after abnormal activation — not ischemia. Can persist days to weeks. Do not reflexively activate the cath lab.
AVNRT. Regular, narrow, fast, with no discernible P waves — they are inside the QRS complexes. Compare V1 with the patient's baseline ECG and the "new" r′ becomes obvious.
CardioNetworks: Googletrans · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons: De-Avnrt ecg2 (CardioNetworks ECGpedia).jpg
Regular at 141 bpm — and it's flutter. An 82-year-old with lung and renal disease; the rhythm is atrial flutter with 2:1 block even though no flutter waves are visible. This is precisely why a regular narrow tachycardia near 150 deserves adenosine as a diagnostic maneuver.
Michael Rosengarten BEng, MD.McGill · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons: E338 (CardioNetworks ECGpedia).jpg
SVT with rate-related aberrancy. The patient goes from sinus into a wide-complex tachycardia at ~130 bpm, and after nine beats the QRS narrows while the rate stays the same. A wide complex that becomes narrow at an unchanged rate is aberrancy, not VT — the bundle recovered.
Michael Rosengarten BEng, MD.McGill · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons: E40 (CardioNetworks ECGpedia).jpg
Multifocal atrial tachycardia. Irregular, with at least three distinct P-wave morphologies and varying PR and PP intervals. Frequently misread as atrial fibrillation — the difference matters, because MAT is treated by fixing the lungs, not by rate-controlling the heart.
Jer5150 · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Multifocal atrial tachycardia - MAT.png

Adenosine as a diagnostic test, not just a treatment

Give it with a rhythm strip running. What the rhythm does in those few seconds of AV block is itself the diagnosis.

Response to adenosineInterpretationWhat to do next
Abrupt termination — and the last event is a P wave after the final QRSAV-node-dependent re-entry: AVNRT or AVRTDefinitive. Post-conversion 12-lead hunting for a delta wave; plan EP referral.
Termination with the last event a QRS (no trailing P)Argues against atrial tachycardia — the drug blocked the node and the circuit died. Still AVNRT/AVRT.Same as above.
Transient AV block that unmasks sawtooth or discrete atrial P waves, then the tachycardia continuesAtrial flutter or focal AT — the atrium is driving, the node was a bystanderSwitch to rate control (IV diltiazem/beta-blocker) and treat the atrial rhythm; consider anticoagulation rules for flutter.
Gradual slowing then gradual re-accelerationSinus tachycardia or an automatic focusStop hunting for SVT — find the cause (fever, PE, hypovolemia, pain, anemia, thyrotoxicosis, withdrawal).
No change whatsoeverInadequate delivery (slow push, small vein, no flush) — or VTRepeat correctly with a proximal large-bore IV, arm elevated, 20 mL flush. If still nothing, reconsider VT.
Degenerates into atrial fibrillationA recognised adenosine effect — reported in about 10% of accessory-pathway-mediated AVRT, with adenosine-induced VF <1%. ESC notes it is more commonly associated with AVRT than AVNRT.Usually self-limited — but catastrophic if there is an accessory pathway, because you have just created pre-excited AF. Have the defibrillator at the bedside for every push.
Adenosine — an endogenous purine nucleoside, not a designed drug. Your own cells release it during ischemia and high workload as a local "slow down" signal; the intravenous bolus simply floods the AV node with the body's own brake. Credit: NEUROtiker · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons: Adenosin.svg. Half-life under 10 seconds — metabolised by adenosine deaminase in red cells and endothelium. That is why it must be a rapid push into a large proximal vein with an immediate 20 mL flush: the drug has to reach the heart before it is destroyed.
Warn the patient before you push. Adenosine reliably produces a few seconds of chest pressure, flushing, dyspnea and a genuine sense of impending doom, plus a frightening pause on the monitor. Ten seconds of warning ("this will feel awful for about five seconds, and then it will be over") converts a traumatic experience into a tolerable one — and stops the patient from pulling out the IV mid-push.
🧮

Brugada criteria — is this wide-complex tachycardia VT or SVT with aberrancy?

Four sequential questions. A "yes" at any step ends the algorithm and diagnoses VT. Only if all four are negative do you call it SVT with aberrant conduction. Check the boxes that are present:

1. Absence of an RS complex in all precordial leads V1–V6 (i.e. positive or negative concordance) VT
2. RS interval >100 ms in any one precordial lead (onset of R to nadir of S) VT
3. AV dissociation present (P waves marching independently, capture or fusion beats) VT
4. Morphology criteria for VT present in both V1–V2 and V6 (see table below) VT
0
PatternV1–V2 features favouring VTV6 features favouring VT
RBBB-like (dominant R in V1)Monophasic R · qR complex · taller LEFT rabbit ear (R > R′) · notched downslopeQS complex, or R/S ratio <1
LBBB-like (dominant S in V1)Initial R wave >30–40 ms · notched/slurred S downstroke (Josephson sign) · onset-of-QRS to S-nadir >60–70 msQS complex, or a qR complex

Brugada P, Brugada J, Mont L, Smeets J, Andries EW. A new approach to the differential diagnosis of a regular tachycardia with a wide QRS complex. Circulation 1991;83:1649–59. Reported in the derivation cohort of 554 tachycardias: sensitivity 98.7%, specificity 96.5%. Independent validation has been substantially less impressive (sensitivity ~89%, specificity ~59%), so treat a "negative" result as reassuring rather than conclusive.

These algorithms adjust probability; they do not license you to treat a wide-complex tachycardia as SVT. In an undifferentiated adult, ~80% of wide-complex tachycardia is VT, rising to >90% with prior MI or structural heart disease, and age >35 alone carries a positive predictive value near 85%. When you are not certain, treat it as VT — that error is survivable, the reverse often is not.
🧮

Vereckei aVR algorithm — the single-lead version

Uses lead aVR only, which makes it faster at the bedside. Same rule: any "yes" = VT; all four negative = SVT with aberrancy.

1. Initial dominant R wave in aVR VT
2. Initial r or q wave >40 ms in aVR VT
3. Notch on the descending limb of a predominantly negative, negative-onset QRS in aVR VT
4. vi/vt ≤ 1 (voltage change in the first 40 ms ÷ voltage change in the last 40 ms) VT
0
Steps 2–4 all measure the same physical thing: how fast the impulse gets moving at the start of the QRS. In SVT with aberrancy the impulse enters via the His–Purkinje system and rockets away — a fast, clean initial deflection. In VT it starts in working myocardium and crawls cell-to-cell before finding the Purkinje network, so the beginning of the QRS is slow and notched while the end is comparatively fast. That inversion of the normal velocity pattern is the vi/vt ≤ 1 rule.

Vereckei A, Duray G, Szénási G, Altemose GT, Miller JM. New algorithm using only lead aVR for differential diagnosis of wide QRS complex tachycardia. Heart Rhythm 2008;5:89–98 — 483 wide-QRS tachycardias (351 VT, 112 SVT, 20 pre-excited) in 313 patients with proven diagnoses. The published abstract reports superiority rather than raw accuracy figures: greater sensitivity and negative predictive value for VT, greater specificity and positive predictive value for SVT, and better overall accuracy than the Brugada algorithm (P = 0.002 and P = 0.007). Widely reproduced teaching figures quote ~96% sensitivity / ~99% specificity, but those numbers are not stated in the abstract — treat them as secondary. Independent validation by non-electrophysiologists has been much weaker, with specificity as low as ~48%.

Presentation & findings — and why each one happens

🩺

Symptoms & signs — frequency and the mechanism behind each

Almost every symptom of SVT is downstream of one hemodynamic fact: at 200 bpm, diastole is brutally short. Diastole is when the ventricle fills and when the coronaries perfuse, so shortening it simultaneously drops stroke volume and drops myocardial oxygen supply — while the rate itself raises oxygen demand. Add the loss of coordinated atrial contribution ("atrial kick", normally 20–30% of filling) and you have the whole symptom complex.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Palpitations — sudden, "switch-like" onset~81%Conscious awareness of rapid, regular ventricular contraction. The abruptness is the diagnostic feature: re-entry is either on or off, with no ramp. Patients often name the exact second it started.
Dizziness / light-headedness~42%Fall in cardiac output → transient cerebral hypoperfusion, worst in the first seconds before vasoconstrictor reflexes compensate.
Dyspnea~35%Short diastole → incomplete LV filling → rising LA pressure → pulmonary venous congestion. Also simple awareness of an inadequate cardiac output.
Neck pounding / "frog sign"frequency uncertain
but specificity 97%, PPV 83%		Cannon A waves. In AVNRT atria and ventricles contract simultaneously, so the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve and blood is fired backwards into the jugular veins. Witnessed neck pulsations were 97% specific (95% CI 90–100%) with a PPV of 83% for SVT, and conferred roughly 7-fold greater odds of typical AVNRT. Secondary sources quote a prevalence of ~51% in typical versus ~25% in atypical AVNRT, but no reliable primary prevalence figure could be verified — so treat this as a highly specific sign of unknown sensitivity, and note it performs poorly at separating AVNRT from AF/flutter.
Chest pain / pressure~20–35%Demand ischemia — rate ↑ demand while shortened diastole ↓ coronary perfusion time. Usually occurs with entirely normal coronaries, but does not exclude CAD.
Anxiety / sense of doomcommon, %-not-establishedSympathetic surge plus the alarming sensation itself. Frequently misdiagnosed as panic disorder for years before an ECG is finally captured during an episode.
Polyuria after the episode~20–50%Elevated atrial pressure stretches atrial myocytes → ANP release → natriuresis and diuresis. A history of "I have to urinate a lot afterwards" is a strongly suggestive clue that the ESC guideline specifically calls out as worth eliciting.
Presyncope~15–25%Same as dizziness, more severe. Commoner in older patients, whose stiffer ventricles and less compliant vasculature tolerate the drop in output poorly.
Frank syncope<15%Either the initial output drop at onset, or a post-conversion sinus pause. In a young patient, syncope with SVT raises concern for a rapidly conducting accessory pathway.
Hypotension / shock<10%Uncommon in a structurally normal heart, which tolerates 200 bpm surprisingly well. Its presence should make you ask what else is wrong — sepsis, hypovolemia, ischemia, pre-existing LV dysfunction, or a wrong diagnosis (VT).
Heart failure signs / cardiomyopathy<10%Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy — weeks to months of incessant or very frequent tachycardia depletes myocardial energy stores and remodels the ventricle. Largely reversible once rhythm is controlled; classically caused by incessant focal AT or permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia.

Palpitations 80.8%, dizziness 42.3% and dyspnea 34.6% are from a cohort of 175 patients undergoing PSVT ablation (PMC9148719). Neck-pounding frequencies (51% typical vs 25% atypical AVNRT) and the polyuria/ANP association are per the 2019 ESC SVT Guidelines and the frog-sign literature. Where a reliable published percentage does not exist, this table says so rather than inventing one — figures marked with a range are approximations synthesised across small series and should be read as "how often you will see it," not as trial data.

The history does most of the diagnostic work — ask these five questions. (1) Did it start instantly, like a switch, or ramp up? Instant = re-entry; ramp = sinus/automatic. (2) Does it stop instantly too? (3) Can you stop it yourself — bearing down, coughing, cold water? A "yes" is nearly diagnostic of AV-node-dependent SVT. (4) Do you urinate a lot afterwards? (5) Does your neck pound? A patient who answers yes to 1, 3 and 5 has AVNRT until the ECG says otherwise.
Syncope during palpitations in a young person is not "just SVT." It demands exclusion of a rapidly conducting accessory pathway, structural heart disease, and inherited channelopathy (long QT, Brugada, CPVT, ARVC). Get a resting 12-lead looking specifically for pre-excitation, QT, and epsilon waves; get an echo; ask about family history of sudden death under 40 and about drowning or unexplained single-vehicle accidents in relatives.
🧪

Interpreting the labs — what moves, why, and what fools you

SVT is an ECG diagnosis; labs exist to find a trigger, exclude a mimic, and make treatment safe. Nothing on this list confirms or excludes SVT itself.

TestWhat SVT does to itMechanism & the trap
TroponinMildly elevated in a large minority — reported in roughly 15–50% depending on assay and rateDemand ischemia, not plaque rupture. Rate-dependent supply–demand mismatch plus myocardial stretch releases troponin through entirely normal coronaries. The trap runs both ways: do not reflexively activate the cath lab for a post-SVT bump, and do not dismiss a rise in someone with genuine risk factors or ongoing pain. Trend it, and let the clinical picture and ECG decide. Elevation in this setting has not been shown to change 30- or 90-day mortality.
TSH (± free T4)Low TSH suggests thyrotoxicosisThyroid hormone increases β-receptor density and sinus automaticity, and shortens atrial refractoriness — it both mimics SVT (sinus tachycardia) and precipitates true atrial arrhythmia. Check it in every new presentation; treating the SVT without treating the thyroid guarantees recurrence.
Potassium & magnesiumOften low, especially post-episodeCatecholamine surge drives K⁺ intracellularly via β₂-stimulated Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, so the potassium you measure after an episode may be spuriously low rather than depleted. Low K⁺ and Mg²⁺ nevertheless prolong repolarisation and promote triggered activity — replete them, but re-check before chasing a large deficit.
CBCAnemia as a driver of sinus tachycardiaLow oxygen-carrying capacity → compensatory tachycardia. A mimic, not a cause of re-entry. Also gives you a baseline before starting anticoagulation if flutter/AF is found.
BMP / creatinineUsually normalNeeded for renally cleared antiarrhythmics (sotalol, dofetilide) and for contrast/ablation planning. Look for the low K⁺/Mg²⁺ above.
β-hCG—Mandatory in any person of childbearing potential before fluoroscopy, cardioversion planning, or antiarrhythmic prescribing. Changes the entire drug list.
BNP / NT-proBNPRises acutely during the episodeAtrial and ventricular stretch releases natriuretic peptides — the same mechanism producing the post-episode polyuria. A high BNP drawn during SVT does not diagnose chronic heart failure.
Toxicology / drug historyVariableCocaine, amphetamines, high-dose caffeine, energy drinks, decongestants, albuterol, theophylline and thyroid supplements all provoke. Digoxin toxicity classically causes atrial tachycardia with block and junctional tachycardia.
Blood gas / lactateLactate may rise with prolonged tachycardiaReflects the output deficit and increased glycolysis, not necessarily sepsis. In MAT, look hard at the pCO₂ and oxygenation — the lungs are the disease.

Imaging & rhythm monitoring — what to order and when

StudyWhen to order itWhat you are looking for
12-lead ECG during tachycardiaAlways, before you treat, if the patient is stable enoughThe single highest-yield test in the whole workup. QRS width, regularity, RP interval, P morphology. Once you convert them, this information is gone forever — get the tracing.
12-lead ECG in sinus rhythmAlways, after conversion and at the clinic visitDelta wave / short PR (pre-excitation), baseline bundle branch block, QT interval, ischemic changes, and the V1 morphology you will compare against for pseudo-R′.
Continuous rhythm strip during adenosineEvery time you push adenosineThe response is the diagnosis (see table above). Pushing adenosine without a recording running wastes the test.
Transthoracic echocardiogramNew SVT diagnosis; any pre-excitation; suspected structural disease; before starting flecainide/propafenoneLV function, valvular disease, congenital lesions (Ebstein anomaly is associated with accessory pathways), and evidence of tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. A normal echo is what permits class IC antiarrhythmics.
Holter, 24–48 hSymptoms occurring dailyRhythm at symptom onset; burden quantification. Useless if episodes are weekly or rarer.
Patch monitor, 7–14 daysSymptoms weekly to monthly — the usual choiceBest yield-per-hassle for typical paroxysmal SVT. Patient-triggered marker plus continuous recording.
Event / loop recorder (30 days)Symptoms less than monthly but at least a few times a yearPatient-activated capture of infrequent events.
Implantable loop recorderRare (<1–2/year) but severe events — syncope, injuryUp to ~3 years of monitoring. Reserved for high-stakes, low-frequency symptoms.
Exercise treadmill testExercise-triggered symptoms; risk-stratifying asymptomatic pre-excitationAbrupt loss of the delta wave at higher heart rates indicates a pathway with a long refractory period — a low-risk pathway. Gradual fading is not the same thing and does not count.
Electrophysiology studyDiagnosis unclear despite monitoring; planning ablation; risk-stratifying asymptomatic pre-excitation; high-risk occupationDefinitive mechanism, inducibility, pathway location and refractory period. Usually performed in the same session as the ablation.
Chest imaging / CTPAOnly if the tachycardia is sinus and you are hunting the causePE, pneumonia, pneumothorax. Do not order this for a diagnosed AVNRT.
Choosing a monitor is a frequency problem, not a preference problem. Match the recording window to the symptom interval: daily → Holter; weekly-to-monthly → 14-day patch; a few times a year → 30-day event recorder; rare but dangerous → implantable loop. Ordering a 24-hour Holter for monthly palpitations is the single most common wasted test in this workup.
🩺 Clinic — outpatient diagnosis, definitive therapy & prevention
Assess

When to suspect it in clinic

🔍

The outpatient presentation — usually a normal patient with a normal exam

The defining clinic problem is that the patient is in sinus rhythm when you see them. Everything therefore hinges on the history and on capturing a tracing. A young, otherwise well patient describing recurrent, abrupt, regular, fast palpitations that stop as suddenly as they start — sometimes with a Valsalva — has SVT until proven otherwise, even with a completely normal resting ECG and exam.

  • Who: AVNRT peaks in the third to fifth decade and affects women about twice as often as men; AVRT presents younger and skews male. Symptom onset in childhood or adolescence suggests an accessory pathway.
  • Triggers to elicit: caffeine and energy drinks, alcohol, sleep deprivation, emotional stress, exercise (especially the recovery phase), position change (bending over), decongestants, stimulants and illicit sympathomimetics, and — in women — menstrual cycle phase and pregnancy.
  • The commonest misdiagnosis: panic attacks. Both cause palpitations, dyspnea, chest tightness and fear. The discriminator is that in SVT the palpitations come first and the anxiety follows, onset and offset are instantaneous, and the rate is high and unwavering; in panic, anxiety builds first and the heart rate ramps and settles gradually. Many patients carry a psychiatric label for years before someone captures a tracing.
  • Physical exam: normal between episodes. During an episode look specifically for regular cannon A waves in the neck (frog sign, favours AVNRT). Document a resting ECG hunting for pre-excitation regardless.
Teach the patient to capture the rhythm themselves. A consumer smartwatch single-lead ECG or a handheld device recorded during an episode frequently settles the diagnosis faster than a monitor you order — and costs nothing. Ask them to also count and record their pulse for 30 seconds during the next event. Any tracing showing a regular narrow tachycardia at 150–250 bpm justifies EP referral.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

The outpatient order set

12-lead ECG (sinus)Every patient, first visit. Hunting for a delta wave and short PR, baseline BBB, QT, and the V1 morphology you will later compare for pseudo-R′. A normal ECG does not exclude SVT — concealed pathways look normal.Always
TSHEvery new presentation. Thyrotoxicosis both mimics and precipitates; treating the rhythm without the thyroid guarantees recurrence.Always
CBC, BMP (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Cr)Every new presentation. Anemia as a mimic; electrolytes as substrate; creatinine before any renally cleared antiarrhythmic.Always
β-hCGAny person of childbearing potential, before fluoroscopy or antiarrhythmic prescribing.If applicable
Ambulatory monitorMatch the device to symptom frequency: daily → 24–48 h Holter; weekly–monthly → 14-day patch; a few per year → 30-day event recorder; rare but syncopal → implantable loop.Diagnosis unconfirmed
Transthoracic echoNew diagnosis; any pre-excitation; suspected structural disease; frequent/incessant tachycardia (looking for tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy); and mandatory before flecainide or propafenone.Most patients
Exercise treadmill testExercise-triggered symptoms, or risk-stratifying asymptomatic pre-excitation (abrupt loss of delta wave at higher rate = low-risk pathway).Selected
EP study referralRecurrent symptomatic SVT (for ablation); undiagnosed tachycardia after monitoring; asymptomatic pre-excitation needing risk stratification; high-risk occupation or competitive athlete.Definitive
Do not order a stress test, CTPA, or D-dimer for a documented regular narrow-complex SVT. Those tests belong to the workup of sinus tachycardia, where the tachycardia is a symptom of something else. Misclassifying SVT as "possible PE" is a common and expensive detour.
Treat

Long-term management

💊

The ladder — and why rung 2 is usually the right answer, not rung 3

Chronic SVT management is unusual in medicine: the definitive cure is safer and more effective than the drugs, so the ladder is not a simple escalation from cheap to expensive. For recurrent symptomatic AVNRT and AVRT, catheter ablation is a Class I recommendation in the 2019 ESC guideline and should be offered early rather than held in reserve.

1
Trigger removal + teach self-termination
Free, immediate, and effective for mild infrequent disease
▾

For infrequent, brief, well-tolerated episodes this may be the whole treatment.

  • Teach the modified Valsalva — this is a skill, not advice. Semi-recumbent at 45°, blow into a 10 mL syringe hard enough to just move the plunger (≈40 mmHg) for 15 seconds, then lie flat immediately and have someone raise both legs to 45° for 15 seconds, then sit back up. Reassess after 60 seconds. In the REVERT trial this converted 43% versus 17% for the standard Valsalva.
  • Other vagal options: cold-water face immersion or an ice pack to the face (diving reflex — especially effective in children), squatting, coughing. Carotid sinus massage is for clinicians only, one side at a time, never in anyone with a carotid bruit, prior stroke/TIA, or known carotid disease.
  • Reduce triggers: caffeine and energy drinks, alcohol, sleep deprivation, stimulant decongestants (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine), and illicit sympathomimetics.
  • Correct anemia, thyrotoxicosis, and hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia.
Straining raises intrathoracic pressure and drops venous return; releasing the strain while simultaneously restoring preload with leg elevation produces a much larger, better-timed baroreceptor-mediated vagal surge. The extra vagal acetylcholine opens the same GIRK potassium channel that adenosine targets, transiently blocking the AV node and collapsing the circuit. The postural modification exists purely to make that reflex bigger.
2
Catheter ablation — the definitive, usually preferred option
Class I for recurrent symptomatic AVNRT and AVRT (ESC 2019)
▾

A day-case procedure under conscious sedation or general anaesthesia. Catheters map the circuit; radiofrequency or cryo-energy destroys one limb of it — the slow pathway in AVNRT, the accessory pathway in AVRT. Cryoablation is often chosen for pathways near the compact AV node because the lesion can be tested reversibly before it is made permanent, reducing AV block risk.

SubstrateAcute successRecurrenceComplicationsMortality
AVNRT97%2%0.3% — vascular, AV block, pericardial effusion0.01%
AVRT (accessory pathway)92%8%1.5% — vascular, AV block, MI, PE, effusion0.1%
Focal atrial tachycardia85%20%1.4% — vascular, AV block, effusion0.1%
Cavotricuspid-isthmus atrial flutter95%10%2% — vascular, stroke, MI, effusion0.2%

Table 11, 2019 ESC SVT Guidelines. Rates for focal AT and AVRT vary substantially with the location of the focus or pathway.

Who should be referred for ablation now, not later: recurrent symptomatic AVNRT or AVRT; anyone who has failed or does not want daily drug therapy; any symptomatic patient with pre-excitation (WPW syndrome); incessant tachycardia or tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy; patients in high-risk occupations (commercial pilots, professional drivers, divers) and competitive athletes; and patients planning pregnancy who have symptomatic SVT — ablating before conception avoids the entire drug-in-pregnancy problem.
The complication that matters for AVNRT ablation is AV block requiring a permanent pacemaker, because the slow pathway lies close to the compact node. Quote it honestly at roughly 0.3% overall for AVNRT in the ESC table (older series report up to ~1%), and mention that cryoablation is used specifically to reduce it. Patients deserve that number before consenting.
3
Chronic drug therapy — if ablation is declined, deferred or unavailable
Full dose ladders below
▾

Choose by comorbidity first, then by tolerability. In a structurally normal heart start with an AV-nodal blocker; reserve class IC agents for when nodal blockers fail and the echo is clean.

If the home dose is unknown (patient can't recall, no records, transfer from outside): restart at the lowest listed starting dose rather than guessing at their prior dose, confirm with the pharmacy or prior notes, and re-titrate upward. Under-dosing a rate-control agent for 48 hours is safe; a doubled beta-blocker or verapamil dose in an unknown patient is not.

Chronic oral drug ladders — start → titration → target/max

AV-nodal blockers — first-line drug therapy in a structurally normal heart

DrugStartTitrationTarget / maxWhy it worksMonitor / alternatives

(max 400 mg)		β₁ blockade → ↓cAMP → ↓If and ↓ICaL in nodal tissue → slows AV nodal conduction, raises the refractory period, and blunts the catecholamine surge that triggers episodes.Once-daily dosing aids adherence. Alt: metoprolol tartrate 25–100 mg BID (max 400/day), atenolol 25–100 mg daily, bisoprolol 2.5–10 mg daily, nadolol 40–120 mg daily (favoured in some athletes for a long half-life).

Class IC antiarrhythmics — only when the heart is structurally normal

Flecainide50 mg PO q12h↑ by 50 mg/dose every ≥4 days100–150 mg q12h
(max 300 mg/day)		Potent sodium-channel blockade with slow dissociation kinetics — acts on fast-response tissue, so it depresses conduction in the atrium and, crucially, in the accessory pathway itself. This is why it treats AVRT at the pathway rather than the node.Requires a normal echo and no coronary disease — the CAST trial showed excess mortality when class IC agents were given post-MI. Sotalol
guidelines disagree		40–80 mg PO q12h↑ every 3 days with ECG80–160 mg q12hCombined non-selective beta-blockade and potassium-channel (IKr) blockade prolonging refractoriness.The two guidelines diverge here. The 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline lists sotalol and dofetilide as Class IIb options, but the 2019 ESC guideline carries the explicit key message: "Do not use sotalol in patients with SVT." "Pill-in-the-pocket" — for infrequent but prolonged episodes

For patients with well-tolerated episodes occurring less often than about monthly, a single dose taken only when an episode starts avoids daily drug exposure entirely. It must be trialled first under observation.

RegimenSingle doseEvidenceCautions
Diltiazem + propranololDiltiazem 120 mg PO + propranolol 80 mg PO, onceConverted up to 94% of patients in the studies cited by the 2019 ESC guideline — the best-supported oral single-dose regimen.Risk of hypotension, transient AV block and rarely syncope. Take it sitting or lying down. Caution in the elderly and in known sinus or AV nodal disease.
Flecainide, single dose3 mg/kg PO, onceAlso effective per ESC 2019, at a lower conversion rate than the above.Structurally normal heart only. First dose observed.
Etripamil nasal spray (CARDAMYST)70 mg (one spray per nostril); may repeat 70 mg once after 10 min; max 140 mg/24 hFDA-approved 2025. In the RAPID trial, 64% converted by 30 minutes vs 31% with placebo; median time to conversion 17 vs 54 minutes.Self-administered sitting down — causes dizziness and syncope. Contraindicated in WPW/pre-excitation, NYHA II–IV heart failure, sick sinus syndrome without a pacemaker, and Mobitz II or higher AV block. Seek emergency care if no improvement 20 min after the second dose.
Etripamil is a short-acting intranasal L-type calcium channel blocker — chemically a verapamil relative engineered for rapid onset and rapid offset. It is the first therapy that lets a patient abort an SVT episode at home without an emergency department visit, which reframes the conversation for patients who refuse ablation. Note its contraindication list mirrors the logic of the whole guide: no AV-nodal blockade in pre-excitation.
Special

Pre-excitation & WPW — including the asymptomatic patient

⚡

The incidental delta wave — what to do with it

Pre-excitation appears on roughly 0.15–0.25% of ECGs. The clinical question is not whether the pathway exists but whether it can conduct fast enough antegrade to be lethal. Sudden death in WPW occurs when atrial fibrillation develops and the pathway — lacking the AV node's protective decremental conduction — passes impulses to the ventricle at rates that degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. The lifetime risk is low (the ESC cites an annual sudden-death risk of about 0.01% per patient-year by age 15 in a paediatric cohort), but it is not zero, and it can be the first symptom.

FindingRisk implicationWhy
SPERRI ≤250 ms (shortest pre-excited R-R during induced AF)HIGH — ablateDirectly measures how fast the pathway can machine-gun the ventricle. The most consistent electrophysiologic predictor of sudden death.
Accessory-pathway antegrade ERP ≤240–250 msHIGH — ablateA short refractory period means the pathway recovers fast enough to conduct nearly every atrial impulse.
Multiple accessory pathways; septal location; inducible AVRT or AF at EP studyHigher riskMore circuits and more substrate for AF initiation.
Abrupt, complete loss of the delta wave during exercise or after procainamideLOW riskDemonstrates a long refractory period — the pathway cannot keep up at fast rates, so it cannot conduct dangerously during AF. Must be abrupt and complete; gradual attenuation does not count and is a common misread.
Intermittent pre-excitation on a resting ECG or HolterTraditionally reassuring — but imperfectThe logic is that beat-to-beat loss implies poor antegrade conduction, and the 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline rates intermittent loss as Class I useful for identifying low risk. However, ESC 2019 explicitly states that "intermittent pre-excitation is now recognized as an imperfect marker of a low-risk AP" — more than one-fifth of such patients have an accessory-pathway ERP <250 ms. Do not use it alone to close the case in a high-stakes patient.
Asymptomatic pre-excitation: the 2019 ESC guideline supports performing an EP study to risk-stratify, and ablation is recommended in asymptomatic patients in whom EP testing identifies high-risk properties. The 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline frames it as Class IIa on three fronts — an EP study "is reasonable" to risk-stratify; ablation "is reasonable" if the study shows high risk including rapidly conducting pre-excited AF; and ablation "is reasonable… if the presence of pre-excitation precludes specific employment (such as with pilots)." It also rates observation without further evaluation as reasonable (Class IIa) — so this is a genuine shared decision, not a mandate. Non-invasive testing comes first, but ESC cautions that its "predictive ability remains modest" and that catecholamine sensitivity limits every test, invasive and non-invasive, including exercise testing. Threshold to proceed is lower in competitive athletes and high-risk occupations (pilots, commercial drivers, divers, military), where an event would endanger others.
Drugs that must never be used chronically in pre-excitation: digoxin, verapamil and diltiazem. All shorten accessory-pathway refractoriness or preferentially block the node, so if the patient develops AF the pathway conducts even faster. If drug therapy is needed in WPW and the heart is structurally normal, flecainide or propafenone is the appropriate choice because they act on the pathway itself.
Comorbid

Comorbidity interactions & drugs to avoid

🔗

How the comorbidity changes both the disease and the drug list

ComorbidityEffect on the arrhythmiaEffect on management
HFrEF (EF <40%)Poorer tolerance of any tachycardia; higher risk of decompensation; tachycardia may itself be causing the low EFAvoid verapamil and diltiazem (negative inotropes) and avoid flecainide/propafenone (proarrhythmic in structural disease). Use beta-blockers already indicated for HF; amiodarone if an antiarrhythmic is unavoidable. Push toward ablation — and remember reversible tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy: recheck the EF 3–6 months after rhythm control.
Asthma / COPDMAT is a marker of severe COPD; hypoxia, hypercapnia and β-agonists all provokeAdenosine can cause bronchospasm — the ESC notes IV adenosine had no airway impact in experimental studies but isolated well-documented bronchospasm reports exist, so use cautiously in asthma and prefer verapamil in severe asthma. Prefer cardioselective beta-blockers (metoprolol, bisoprolol) if a beta-blocker is needed; avoid propranolol and propafenone's beta-blocking effect. For MAT, treat the lungs — the rhythm follows.
Coronary artery disease / prior MIDemand ischemia during episodes; raises the pre-test probability that a wide-complex tachycardia is VT (>90%)Class IC agents are contraindicated (CAST). Beta-blockers are doubly indicated. Lower threshold to evaluate a troponin rise as genuine rather than reflexive demand.
Pre-excitation / WPWAF becomes potentially lethalNo digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem, or chronic AV-nodal monotherapy. Flecainide/propafenone if drugs are needed and the heart is structurally normal. Ablation is the answer.
PregnancySVT frequency often increases (↑plasma volume, ↑heart rate, ↑catecholamines)Vagal maneuvers then adenosine are Class I and safe in all trimesters. Cardioversion "seems safe in all phases of pregnancy" — check the fetal heart rate afterwards. β₁-selective blockers are preferred except atenolol, which is associated with small-for-gestational-age infants and is specifically singled out as not a class effect. Flecainide or propafenone should be considered for prevention per ESC 2019 — including in WPW without ischemic or structural heart disease. Avoid amiodarone. Defer ablation where possible; if unavoidable, use zero- or minimal-fluoroscopy technique, ideally after the first trimester. The best move by far is to ablate before conception.
ThyrotoxicosisPrecipitates and perpetuates; a common reversible driverTreat the thyroid or the arrhythmia will recur. Beta-blockers do double duty. Be cautious attributing everything to SVT before TSH returns.
Chronic kidney diseaseElectrolyte shifts create substrateDose-adjust or avoid sotalol and dofetilide (renally cleared, QT-prolonging). Watch K⁺ and Mg²⁺ closely around dialysis.
Heart transplantDenervated heartProfound supersensitivity to adenosine — prolonged asystole can result. If used at all, start at a markedly reduced dose with pacing capability immediately available; many centres avoid it entirely.
Sick sinus syndrome / conduction diseaseTachy-brady physiologyAV-nodal blockers may unmask severe bradycardia or long post-conversion pauses. May require pacing before rate-control drugs can be used safely.
ElderlySymptoms more severe (dizziness, presyncope) due to less compliant circulationStart every drug at the lowest dose. Higher risk of hypotension with IV CCBs and of constipation with verapamil. Ablation is well tolerated and should not be withheld on age alone.
Drugs to avoid — the consolidated list.
• Pre-excited AF (irregular, wide): digoxin, beta-blockers, diltiazem, verapamil and IV amiodarone are all ESC 2019 Class III (Level B) — not recommended and potentially harmful; adenosine likewise. Use procainamide, ibutilide, or electricity.
• Sotalol in SVT generally: ESC 2019 key message — "Do not use sotalol in patients with SVT" (the 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline is more permissive at Class IIb; the guidelines genuinely disagree).
• Any WPW patient, chronically: digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem.
• HFrEF: verapamil, diltiazem, flecainide, propafenone.
• Structural or ischemic heart disease: flecainide, propafenone (CAST).
• Undifferentiated wide-complex tachycardia: verapamil and diltiazem — they cause catastrophic hypotension and degeneration if the rhythm is actually VT.
• Severe asthma: adenosine (prefer verapamil), non-selective beta-blockers.
• Concurrent IV beta-blocker + IV calcium channel blocker: additive hypotension and bradycardia — the ESC calls for explicit caution. Space them and reassess in between.
Monitor

Follow-up & titration cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

SituationIntervalWhat you are checking
Starting or titrating a beta-blocker or CCB2–4 weeksResting HR and BP, symptom burden and episode frequency, fatigue, constipation (verapamil), bronchospasm.
Starting flecainide or propafenoneECG at 3–5 days, then with each dose changeQRS duration — reduce or stop if it widens >25% above baseline. Also exercise ECG in selected patients to expose use-dependent QRS widening at high rates.
Starting sotalol or dofetilideECG before and with each dose; often in-hospitalQTc — stop if >500 ms. Recheck renal function and K⁺/Mg²⁺.
Post-ablationVisit at 4–8 weeks; sooner if symptoms recurAccess-site complications, recurrence of palpitations, and the resting ECG (documenting loss of pre-excitation after pathway ablation). Palpitations in the first weeks are common and often benign ectopy rather than true recurrence.
Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathyRepeat echo at 3–6 monthsEF recovery after rhythm control — usually substantial and often complete. Confirms the diagnosis retrospectively.
Stable on chronic therapy, no ablationEvery 6–12 monthsEpisode frequency and tolerability, drug side effects, ECG, and a renewed conversation about ablation — many patients say yes on the second or third ask.
Driving and occupation. The 2019 ESC guideline includes a dedicated table on driving with SVT. In general, private drivers with well-controlled or ablated SVT face minimal restriction, while commercial licence holders and safety-critical occupations face far stricter requirements and often need documented ablation before returning to work. Rules are jurisdiction-specific — check your local licensing authority rather than quoting a number from memory, and document the discussion.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B recommendations relevant to this population

There is no USPSTF recommendation to screen for SVT — it is symptom-detected, and the Task Force has not addressed it. What follows are the Grade A and B services that apply to the typical SVT patient as a general-medicine patient, plus the cardiovascular screening that changes SVT management specifically.

GradeRecommendationPopulation & relevance here
AScreen for hypertensionAdults ≥18, with office measurement confirmed outside the clinical setting before starting treatment. Hypertension drives atrial remodelling and coexists with the CCBs/beta-blockers you may already be prescribing.
ATobacco cessation counselling + pharmacotherapyAll adults. Nicotine is a direct sympathomimetic trigger; smoking also drives the COPD that underlies MAT.
BScreen for unhealthy alcohol useAdults ≥18. Alcohol is one of the most commonly identified and most easily modified triggers.
BStatin for primary prevention of CVDAdults 40–75 with ≥1 CVD risk factor and 10-year risk ≥10%. Relevant because established CAD forbids class IC antiarrhythmics.
BScreen for prediabetes and type 2 diabetesAdults 35–70 with overweight/obesity.
BNote: OSA screening in asymptomatic adults is Grade I (insufficient evidence)Not a screening recommendation — but symptomatic OSA evaluation is clinically warranted in patients with nocturnal arrhythmia, and treating it reduces atrial arrhythmia burden.

Disease-specific prevention that actually works here: eliminating stimulant triggers, correcting thyroid disease and anemia, treating OSA when symptomatic, maintaining potassium and magnesium, and — most effectively — curing the substrate with ablation. Routine immunisations apply as for any adult; there is no SVT-specific vaccine indication.

Escalate

When to send to the ED

🚑

Red flags — don't manage these in clinic

Send to the emergency department now if any of these are present:
  • SBP <90 mmHg, or any symptomatic hypotension during the tachycardia
  • Ongoing chest pain, dyspnea at rest, or new pulmonary edema during the episode
  • Syncope — with or during palpitations, at any age
  • Altered mental status or any sign of shock
  • Wide-complex tachycardia of any kind, or an irregular wide-complex rhythm (possible pre-excited AF)
  • Tachycardia that will not terminate after correctly performed vagal maneuvers, or that has been sustained for hours
  • New pre-excitation with symptoms, especially syncope or a family history of sudden death
  • Suspected tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy — new heart-failure symptoms with an incessant tachycardia
  • Rate persistently >220 bpm, or a very young/very old patient tolerating the rate poorly

Everything else — recurrent, self-terminating, well-tolerated episodes in a structurally normal heart — is an outpatient EP referral, not an emergency. Give the patient a written plan for the next episode (modified Valsalva technique, when to call, when to go in), and make the referral before they leave.

🛏️ Wards — acute termination & inpatient management
Admit

Who actually needs admission

📋

Most converted SVT goes home from the ED — these are the exceptions

An otherwise healthy patient whose AVNRT converted with adenosine, who feels well, whose post-conversion ECG shows no pre-excitation and no ischemia, and who has a follow-up plan, does not need admission. Admit for the reasons below, and be explicit in your note about which one applies.

Admit forThreshold / detail
Failure to convertTachycardia persisting after vagal maneuvers + a full adenosine sequence + a second-line agent, or requiring cardioversion to break.
Hemodynamic compromise at any pointSBP <90 mmHg, symptomatic hypotension, syncope, altered mental status, or signs of shock — even if now resolved.
Ischemia that looks realOngoing chest pain after conversion, ischemic ST changes that persist in sinus rhythm, or a rising troponin with a convincing story. A small post-SVT troponin bump with a clean ECG and resolved pain is not, by itself, an admission.
New or decompensated heart failurePulmonary edema during the episode; suspected tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy needing inpatient echo and diuresis.
Pre-excited AF or newly discovered WPW with syncopeAdmit, monitor, and get electrophysiology involved. This group needs urgent risk stratification and usually inpatient or expedited ablation.
Wide-complex tachycardia of uncertain mechanismAdmit to telemetry until VT is excluded.
Initiation of a monitored antiarrhythmicSotalol and dofetilide require in-hospital initiation with serial QTc.
Significant comorbidity or a serious precipitantSepsis, PE, GI bleed, thyroid storm, severe electrolyte derangement, digoxin toxicity, decompensated COPD driving MAT. Here the SVT is the smoke, not the fire.
Very frequent recurrenceMultiple episodes in the same visit, or incessant tachycardia.
Social / accessNo reliable follow-up, lives alone far from care, unable to return if it recurs.
Orders

Admission order set

🧪

What to order on arrival

Continuous telemetryAll admitted SVT. Set alarms; ask explicitly for recorded strips of any recurrence — the strip is worth more than the nurse's description.Immediate
12-lead ECG ×2During tachycardia (if still in it) and after conversion. The post-conversion tracing is where you find the delta wave.Immediate
Defibrillator/pads at bedsideBefore pushing adenosine, and for anyone with pre-excitation or hemodynamic borderline status. Adenosine can precipitate AF — in WPW that is an emergency.Immediate
Two large-bore IVs, proximalAntecubital or more central. Adenosine given through a small distal hand vein frequently "fails" for purely pharmacokinetic reasons.Immediate
BMP, Mg²⁺, CBC, TSHOn admission. Repletion targets: K⁺ >4.0 mEq/L, Mg²⁺ >2.0 mg/dL.Admit
TroponinOnly if chest pain, ischemic ECG changes, or risk factors — and interpret it as demand ischemia unless the story says otherwise. Trend rather than acting on a single value.Selective
β-hCGAny person of childbearing potential, before imaging or antiarrhythmics.If applicable
Transthoracic echoNew diagnosis, any pre-excitation, hemodynamic compromise, suspected cardiomyopathy, or before starting a class IC agent.Within 24 h
Electrophysiology consultPre-excitation of any kind; recurrent or refractory SVT; incessant tachycardia; anyone who is an ablation candidate — which is most of them. Call early; it changes disposition.Day 1
Hold the offendersStop stimulant decongestants, caffeine, theophylline where possible; review for digoxin toxicity; hold QT-prolonging drugs if starting sotalol/dofetilide.Admit
Treat

Acute termination — the ladder

💊

Stable, regular, narrow-complex: vagal → adenosine → nodal blocker → electricity

Ask the stability question first, every time. Per the AHA algorithm, "unstable" means the tachyarrhythmia is causing: hypotension · acutely altered mental status · signs of shock · ischemic chest discomfort · acute heart failure. If any is present → immediate synchronized cardioversion, sedating whenever feasible. Do not work through the ladder in an unstable patient.
The acute pathway. Note the two red boxes on the right — a regular wide-complex rhythm is treated as VT, and an irregular wide-complex rhythm is treated as pre-excited AF. Both are exits from the SVT algorithm, not steps within it.
1
Vagal maneuvers — do them properly
Free, instant, ~43% effective when done right
▾

Modified Valsalva (REVERT technique) — the version to use:

  1. Position the patient semi-recumbent at 45°.
  2. Have them blow into a 10 mL syringe hard enough to just move the plunger — roughly 40 mmHg — for 15 seconds.
  3. Immediately lay them flat and have an assistant raise both legs to 45° for 15 seconds.
  4. Return them to semi-recumbent and reassess the rhythm at 60 seconds.

Other options: ice-water/cold-pack to the face (diving reflex — the best choice in children and infants); coughing; squatting. Carotid sinus massage: 5–10 s, one side only, with continuous ECG — contraindicated with a carotid bruit, prior stroke/TIA, or known carotid stenosis. Never use eyeball pressure — it risks retinal injury and is obsolete.

All vagal maneuvers deliver acetylcholine to the AV node, which opens the same GIRK/IKAdo potassium channel adenosine targets. The postural modification works because the strain phase drops venous return, and releasing it while simultaneously restoring preload with leg elevation produces a much larger and better-timed baroreflex vagal surge than simply stopping the strain.
REVERT (Lancet 2015) randomised 433 patients: sinus restored in 93/214 (43%) with the modified maneuver versus 37/214 (17%) with the standard Valsalva, with no serious adverse events — an NNT of about 4. Most "failed vagal maneuvers" are simply maneuvers performed without the postural component. Teach the patient the technique before discharge; it is a therapy they can carry home.
2
Adenosine — diagnostic and therapeutic in one push
6 → 12 → (18) mg, rapid IV push with immediate flush
▾
DrugStartEscalationMaxWhy it worksCautions / alternatives
Adenosine6 mg rapid IV push + immediate 20 mL NS flush, arm elevated12 mg after 1–2 min if no effectAHA: second dose 12 mg.
ESC 2019: sequence up to 18 mg		A1 receptor → Gi → opens GIRK/IKAdo (K⁺ out, cell hyperpolarizes) and inhibits adenylyl cyclase (↓cAMP → ↓ICaL) → several seconds of complete AV block that collapses the re-entry circuit.Halve the dose (start 3 mg) if given through a central line, or if the patient takes dipyridamole or carbamazepine (both potentiate it). Heart transplant: denervation supersensitivity — markedly reduce or avoid. Caution in asthma (prefer verapamil in severe asthma). Theophylline and caffeine are competitive antagonists — these patients may need higher doses or a different drug.

Technique is the drug. Half-life is under 10 seconds, so failures are usually delivery failures:

  • Large, proximal vein (antecubital or above) — not a hand vein.
  • Stopcock technique: adenosine and a 20 mL flush on a three-way stopcock, pushed back-to-back as fast as possible. Two-person technique.
  • Elevate the arm during and after the push.
  • Rhythm strip running — the response is the diagnosis.
  • Warn the patient about several seconds of chest pressure, flushing, dyspnea and a sense of doom.
Do not give adenosine if the rhythm is irregular and wide. That is pre-excited AF, and blocking the node drives conduction down the accessory pathway. Also avoid it in second- or third-degree AV block or sick sinus syndrome without a pacemaker. Adenosine itself can induce atrial fibrillation — reported in about 10% of accessory-pathway-mediated AVRT (adenosine-induced VF <1%), and the ESC notes it occurs more commonly with AVRT than AVNRT. Usually transient and benign; potentially catastrophic in a patient with an accessory pathway. Defibrillator at the bedside, always.
3
IV calcium channel blocker or beta-blocker
If vagal + adenosine fail, or the rhythm recurs immediately
▾
DrugStartRepeat / titrationMaxWhy it worksCautions
Diltiazem IV0.25 mg/kg IV over 2 min (≈20 mg average)0.35 mg/kg over 2 min after 15 min if neededInfusion 5–15 mg/h for rate controlBlocks the L-type calcium current that generates the AV node's action potential — directly suppresses the circuit's nodal limb.Hypotension is the main risk. Give slowly; consider IV calcium gluconate 1 g pretreatment in borderline BP. Avoid in HFrEF (EF <40%), suspected VT, and pre-excited AF.
Verapamil IV5–10 mg (0.075–0.15 mg/kg) IV over 2 minMay repeat after 15–30 min~20–30 mg totalSame L-type calcium blockade; slightly more negatively inotropic than diltiazem.Same contraindications. Terminates SVT in 64–98% of patients per the ESC guideline, at the cost of more hypotension than adenosine.
Metoprolol IV2.5–5 mg IV over 2 minRepeat q5–10 min15 mg total (given as 2.5 mg boluses per ESC)β₁ blockade → ↓cAMP → ↓ICaL and ↓If in nodal tissue.Better at slowing than terminating. Contraindicated in decompensated heart failure and severe bronchospasm.
Esmolol IV500 mcg/kg bolus over 1 minInfusion 50 mcg/kg/min, ↑ by 50 every 4 min300 mcg/kg/minSame β₁ mechanism, but a 9-minute half-life.The right beta-blocker when you are unsure it will be tolerated — if it drops the blood pressure, stopping the infusion fixes it within minutes. Do not stack an IV calcium channel blocker onto an IV beta-blocker (or vice versa) without deliberate thought — the ESC guideline warns of potentiated hypotension and bradycardia. If the first agent failed, reassess the diagnosis before adding the second; consider that this may be atrial flutter, atrial tachycardia, or VT rather than a refractory AVNRT.
4
Synchronized cardioversion
Immediately if unstable; electively if drugs fail
▾

Synchronize. Press SYNC and confirm the machine is marking each R wave before charging. An unsynchronized shock delivered on the T wave can induce ventricular fibrillation. Re-press SYNC before every subsequent shock — most defibrillators reset to unsynchronized after each delivery.

RhythmEnergy (2025 AHA)Notes
Narrow-complex tachycardia (SVT)100 JSynchronized.
Atrial flutter200 JCOR 2b, LOE C-LD — an initial setting of 200 J "may be reasonable."
Atrial fibrillation200 JCOR 2a, LOE B-R — at least 200 J initially "is reasonable" with any US-approved biphasic waveform.
Monomorphic VT100 JSynchronized.
Polymorphic VT / torsadesUNSYNCHRONIZED high-energy defibrillationThe machine cannot find a reliable R wave in a chaotic rhythm and will simply hang waiting while the patient deteriorates.
These numbers changed in 2025 — check your habits. The familiar ACLS teaching of "50–100 J for narrow regular, 120–200 J for AF, 100 J for wide regular" has been superseded by the 2025 AHA Electrical Cardioversion Algorithm above, and the 2025 guidance explicitly discourages low-energy shocks. Note also that the 2025 Tachyarrhythmia algorithm adds: use your specific device's recommended level where one exists, and if it is not known, use the maximum energy setting.

Have at the bedside before you shock (per the algorithm): oxygen-saturation monitor, suction device, IV line, and intubation equipment. The algorithm also notes that immediate cardioversion is generally not needed if the rate is ≤150/min, and that with a rate >150/min you should prepare for immediate cardioversion while allowing a brief medication trial.

Sedation: sedate whenever feasible in a conscious patient. The AHA algorithm notes that "effective regimens have included a sedative (eg, diazepam) with or without an analgesic agent (eg, fentanyl)" and that "many experts recommend anesthesia if service is readily available"; in practice most units use etomidate, propofol or midazolam ± a short-acting opioid, with airway equipment and someone whose only job is the airway. If synchronization is delayed and the patient is critical, go straight to unsynchronized shocks. Do not delay cardioversion for sedation in a peri-arrest patient.

Anticoagulation: AVNRT and AVRT are not thromboembolic rhythms and cardioversion needs no anticoagulation. Atrial flutter and AF follow the standard rules — if the rhythm has been present ≥48 hours or is of unknown duration, either 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation beforehand or a TEE to exclude thrombus, plus 4 weeks after. Do not let a rhythm you assumed was AVNRT turn out to be flutter after you shock it.

Danger

Pre-excited AF — the scenario that kills

☠️

Irregular + wide + very fast = stop and think

Atrial fibrillation in a patient with an accessory pathway is a different disease from ordinary AF. The AV node normally protects the ventricle by conducting decrementally — the faster you drive it, the more it blocks. An accessory pathway has no such property. It conducts one-to-one until it hits its refractory period, so atrial rates of 400–600 can reach the ventricle at rates well over 250 bpm and degenerate into ventricular fibrillation.

Recognize it byDetail
Irregularly irregularThe atrial rhythm is fibrillation — the ventricular response cannot be regular.
Wide, and varying in width beat to beatEach beat reaches the ventricle via the pathway (very wide, pure delta), the node (narrow, no delta), or both (fusion) — so the QRS morphology changes constantly. This is the single most specific feature.
Very fast — often >200, sometimes >250 bpmFaster than the AV node would ever permit.
Known WPW, or a delta wave on an old ECGLook for it; ask the family.
Absolutely contraindicated: adenosine · verapamil · diltiazem · beta-blockers · digoxin. Each blocks the AV node and shunts more conduction down the accessory pathway, accelerating the ventricular rate toward VF. The 2019 ESC guideline rates digoxin, beta-blockers, diltiazem, verapamil and amiodarone all as Class III (Level B) — "not recommended and potentially harmful" in pre-excited AF. The inclusion of IV amiodarone in that list is the part many clinicians have not absorbed: older teaching treated it as a safe fallback, and it is not.
TreatmentDoseEndpointWhy it works
Unstable → synchronized cardioversionPer device recommendation; if unknown, maximum energySinus rhythmImmediate and definitive. Urgent cardioversion is usually required, and the threshold to use electricity should be low.
Procainamide IV
(preferred drug)		20–50 mg/min infusionStop at any of: arrhythmia suppressed · hypotension · QRS widens >50% · max 17 mg/kg.
Maintenance 1–4 mg/min		Sodium-channel blockade that prolongs refractoriness in the accessory pathway itself — it slows conduction down the dangerous limb rather than the protective one. Avoid with prolonged QT or CHF.
Ibutilide IV1 mg over 10 min; may repeat once after 10 minConversionPotassium-channel blocker; ESC 2019 rates ibutilide or procainamide as "should be considered" (IIa) in stable pre-excited AF. Requires 4 h of monitoring for torsades and normal K⁺/Mg²⁺.
Flecainide / propafenone IVPer local protocolConversion"May be considered" (IIb) per ESC 2019 — same sodium-channel logic as procainamide.

After the emergency: every patient who has had pre-excited AF needs electrophysiology involvement and, in nearly all cases, accessory pathway ablation before discharge or urgently thereafter. Having had one episode is itself the risk factor.

Variants

The other rhythms on your telemetry

🔀

Focal AT, MAT and junctional tachycardia — different rules

RhythmAcute managementThe key difference
Focal atrial tachycardiaAdenosine may transiently terminate some (triggered/adenosine-sensitive foci) but usually only unmasks it. IV beta-blocker or IV diltiazem/verapamil for rate control. ESC 2019: if these fail, IV ibutilide (IIa), or IV flecainide/propafenone, or IV amiodarone (IIb). Cardioversion if drugs fail.The AV node is a bystander. Nodal blockade controls the ventricular rate but does not stop the atrium. Ablation is recommended for recurrent focal AT, especially if incessant or causing cardiomyopathy.
Multifocal atrial tachycardiaTreat the lungs, not the heart. Correct hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis and infection; reduce β-agonist and theophylline load; correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺. IV magnesium can help even when the level is normal. If rate control is genuinely needed: metoprolol has been shown superior to verapamil and beta-blockers may be used with caution when there is no respiratory decompensation, sinus node dysfunction, or AV block; verapamil is the fallback when the airways forbid a beta-blocker. IV metoprolol or verapamil is Class IIa (2015 ACC/AHA/HRS).Cardioversion does not work — there is no single circuit to break, just multiple automatic foci. Shocking MAT is a classic error, and antiarrhythmics in general are unhelpful. Note the double bind: beta-blockers are risky in bronchospasm, but verapamil can worsen hypoxemia by blunting hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. Neither is a substitute for fixing the lungs.
Junctional ectopic / accelerated junctionalFind and remove the cause: digoxin toxicity, recent cardiac surgery, myocarditis, catecholamine excess, ischemia. Correct electrolytes. Treat digoxin toxicity with digoxin-specific Fab if indicated.Automatic, not re-entrant — cardioversion is ineffective and, in digoxin toxicity, dangerous.
Atrial flutterRate control (diltiazem, beta-blocker), or conversion with ibutilide/dofetilide or low-energy cardioversion. Apply AF anticoagulation rules. Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is highly effective for typical flutter.Notoriously drug-resistant to rate control compared with AF. A regular narrow tachycardia near 150 bpm is flutter until proven otherwise.
Sinus tachycardia (physiological)Do not treat the rate. Find the cause: fever, sepsis, pain, hypovolemia, bleeding, PE, hypoxia, anemia, thyrotoxicosis, beta-blocker withdrawal, anxiety, alcohol/caffeine, illicit stimulants, β-agonists.The tachycardia is the compensation. Blocking it removes the patient's ability to maintain cardiac output and can precipitate collapse. ESC: "physiological sinus tachycardia is treated by identifying and eliminating the cause."
Inappropriate sinus tachycardia (IST)Reassurance first — the prognosis is benign and it does not cause tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. ESC 2019 changed the drug of choice to ivabradine ± a beta-blocker (Class IIa); ivabradine 5 mg PO BID, up to 7.5 mg BID, preferably co-administered with a beta-blocker.A diagnosis of exclusion (of POTS, sinus node re-entry, and focal AT from the superior crista or right superior PV): resting rate >100 with a Holter mean >90 bpm. ESC 2019 removed verapamil/diltiazem and catheter ablation as recommended therapy — a change from prior practice. Ivabradine is a CYP3A4 substrate and is contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Junctional tachycardia. Narrow QRS, fast, with no preceding P waves — the AV junction has taken over as pacemaker. In an adult on the wards this should prompt an immediate question about digoxin toxicity, recent cardiac surgery, or myocarditis. It is automatic, not re-entrant, so cardioversion will not help.
James Heilman, MD · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons: Junctional Tachycardia.jpg
Before you treat any tachycardia, ask: "is this rhythm the problem, or the response to the problem?" Sinus tachycardia and MAT are responses. AVNRT and AVRT are problems. Treating a response is how patients get hurt.
