Escalate

When to call the ICU

⬆️

Concrete transfer triggers

Transfer to ICU / step-down for any of:
  • SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 mmHg persisting after conversion attempts, or requiring any vasopressor
  • Requiring a continuous antiarrhythmic infusion — esmolol, diltiazem, amiodarone, procainamide — with titration needs
  • Two or more cardioversions in 24 h, or recurrence within minutes of each conversion
  • Pre-excited AF, or any wide-complex tachycardia not yet excluded as VT
  • Incessant tachycardia that cannot be interrupted, particularly with a falling EF
  • New pulmonary edema requiring non-invasive ventilation, or any need for intubation
  • Lactate rising or clinical hypoperfusion (cool, mottled, oliguric <0.5 mL/kg/h) attributable to the rhythm
  • Ongoing ischemia — dynamic ST changes or a climbing troponin with pain
  • Post-conversion pauses >3–4 seconds or symptomatic bradycardia suggesting sick sinus syndrome — may need temporary pacing
  • Sedation for repeated cardioversions in a patient with a difficult airway or significant comorbidity
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness criteria — and what has to be in the discharge packet

Ready for discharge when all of these are true:

  • In sustained sinus rhythm for a reasonable observation period, with no recurrence on telemetry
  • Hemodynamically stable off all IV antiarrhythmics — SBP >100, HR 60–100, no orthostatic symptoms
  • Post-conversion 12-lead reviewed and documented, specifically for pre-excitation and ischemic changes
  • Electrolytes corrected: K⁺ >4.0, Mg²⁺ >2.0
  • Any reversible precipitant identified and addressed (thyroid, anemia, sepsis, drug, electrolyte)
  • Echo obtained if indicated, and reviewed
  • EP follow-up arranged with a date, or ablation scheduled — not "call the office"
  • Patient has been taught the modified Valsalva and given written return precautions
  • Oral regimen tolerated for at least one dosing interval, with side effects reviewed
Do not discharge a patient with newly documented pre-excitation and syncope, ongoing wide-complex tachycardia of unclear mechanism, an unexplained rising troponin, a QTc >500 ms on a new antiarrhythmic, or recurrent SVT that has not been controlled — regardless of how well they look at the moment.

Home — the default

The great majority. Converted, stable, structurally normal heart, EP follow-up booked, Valsalva taught, triggers reviewed.

Home + expedited ablation

Symptomatic pre-excitation, recurrent SVT failing drugs, or high-risk occupation. Home with a date, not a referral letter.

Home health

Rarely needed for SVT alone. Consider for frail elderly on a new nodal blocker needing BP/HR checks, or for IV access care.

SNF

Only when a comorbidity drives it — deconditioning after a prolonged stay, fall with injury during a syncopal episode, or new functional decline. SVT itself does not generate a skilled need.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Essentially never for SVT. Applies if a complication — embolic stroke after flutter cardioversion, anoxic injury after arrest — leaves a rehabilitation need with ≥3 h/day tolerance.

Palliative / goals of care

When SVT is a recurrent burden in advanced illness. Focus shifts to symptom control and avoiding repeat admissions; discuss whether repeated cardioversion aligns with goals.

The discharge conversation that prevents the readmission

  • Name the diagnosis out loud. "You have SVT — an extra electrical circuit in your heart. It is not a heart attack, and it does not mean your heart is damaged." Many patients have carried an anxiety label for years; this conversation is therapeutic.
  • Teach and rehearse the modified Valsalva before they leave the building.
  • Explain that ablation is a cure, with roughly a 97% success rate for AVNRT, and that choosing it is reasonable even for infrequent episodes.
  • Return precautions: chest pain, syncope, an episode lasting beyond 20–30 minutes despite maneuvers, or shortness of breath at rest.
  • Trigger list in writing: caffeine, energy drinks, alcohol, decongestants, sleep deprivation, stimulants.
🫀 ICU — refractory arrhythmia, infusions & the critically ill patient
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When SVT belongs in the unit — and when the SVT is not the problem

Isolated AVNRT in a structurally normal heart almost never requires intensive care; it converts and the patient goes home. SVT reaches the ICU by one of three routes, and distinguishing them determines the entire plan.

Route to the ICUWhat it looks likeWhat actually needs treating
1. The arrhythmia itself is decompensating the patientRefractory or incessant SVT with hypotension, ischemia, pulmonary edema, or a falling EF; repeated cardioversionsThe rhythm. Infusions, repeat cardioversion, urgent EP involvement.
2. The patient is critically ill and the tachycardia is a symptomSeptic shock, PE, hypovolemia, respiratory failure, thyroid storm, withdrawal — with a fast rhythm on the monitorThe underlying illness. Rate-controlling a compensatory tachycardia removes the patient's compensation and can precipitate arrest. Verify the rhythm is genuinely not sinus before you treat it.
3. The rhythm is dangerous by naturePre-excited AF, wide-complex tachycardia of unknown mechanism, post-cardiac-surgery junctional ectopic tachycardiaImmediate definitive therapy and expert consultation.
Numeric ICU admission triggers: SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 despite conversion attempts · any vasopressor requirement · need for a titrated antiarrhythmic infusion · ≥2 cardioversions in 24 h or immediate re-initiation after each · pre-excited AF · undifferentiated wide-complex tachycardia · lactate >2 mmol/L with hypoperfusion attributable to the rhythm · urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h · new hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring NIV or intubation · post-conversion pauses >3–4 s or symptomatic bradycardia potentially needing temporary pacing.
In the ICU, the default assumption for a wide-complex tachycardia is VT. Critically ill patients have every risk factor for it — ischemia, electrolyte derangement, catecholamines, structural disease, QT-prolonging drugs. Giving verapamil or diltiazem to a patient in VT because it "looked like SVT with aberrancy" causes profound hypotension and can be fatal. If you are not certain, treat as VT: procainamide or amiodarone, or electricity.

🩸

Lines, leads and targets

ItemIndicationWhy
Arterial lineAny titrated antiarrhythmic infusion; recurrent cardioversion; shockBeat-to-beat pressure during procainamide or diltiazem infusion, when hypotension is the rate-limiting toxicity. Cuff pressures are unreliable at rate >180.

K⁺, Mg²⁺ q6–12 hAll patients on antiarrhythmics or with recurrent arrhythmiaTargets K⁺ >4.0 mEq/L and Mg²⁺ >2.0 mg/dL. This is the cheapest antiarrhythmic in the unit and the most frequently neglected.

Infusions, antiarrhythmics & pressors

💉

Rate and rhythm infusions — receptor, dose, titration

Vasopressors — when the rhythm has caused the shock

Pressors are a bridge to definitive rhythm control, not a substitute for it. If the tachycardia is causing the hypotension, the answer is cardioversion — but you may need pressure to survive the sedation.

AgentReceptorsDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick it
PhenylephrinePure α₁0.1–1.5 mcg/kg/min (or 50–200 mcg boluses)↑SVR, reflex ↓HR, no direct chronotropyThe thinking choice here. Raises pressure without adding β-stimulation to an already-tachycardic heart, and the baroreflex slowing it produces can itself help terminate the SVT.
Norepinephrineα₁ >> β₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑SVR, mild ↑contractility, minimal ↑HRDefault when shock is multifactorial or septic. Preferred over dopamine, which is more arrhythmogenic.
VasopressinV₁ receptors0.03 units/min fixed↑SVR, no β-effect at allCatecholamine-sparing add-on when you want pressure without any chronotropic stimulus.
Avoid: dopamine, epinephrine, dobutamine, isoproterenolβ₁/β₂ agonism—↑↑HR, proarrhythmicβ-agonism accelerates the AV node, shortens refractoriness and can accelerate or re-initiate the tachycardia. Reserve for genuine cardiogenic shock where inotropy is unavoidable, and only after rhythm control has failed.
The pressor choice in tachyarrhythmic shock is a receptor question. Every β₁ agonist you infuse is working against your antiarrhythmic — increasing cAMP in exactly the nodal tissue you are trying to suppress. A pure α₁ agonist raises perfusion pressure and, through the baroreflex, adds vagal tone to the AV node. Phenylephrine has genuinely terminated AVNRT for this reason.
Rescue

Electrical & advanced therapy

⚡

Cardioversion, pacing and the refractory patient

Synchronized cardioversion in the unit

  • Press SYNC and confirm R-wave markers before every shock — most defibrillators revert to unsynchronized after each delivery.
  • Energy (2025 AHA Electrical Cardioversion Algorithm): narrow-complex tachycardia 100 J · atrial flutter 200 J · atrial fibrillation 200 J · monomorphic VT 100 J · polymorphic VT unsynchronized defibrillation. The 2025 guidance explicitly discourages low-energy shocks — the older "start at 50 J" habit is obsolete. Where a device publishes its own recommended level, use it; if unknown, use the maximum setting.
  • Polymorphic/irregular wide-complex: defibrillate, unsynchronized. The machine cannot find an R wave and will simply refuse to fire while the patient deteriorates.
  • Sedation: etomidate, propofol or midazolam ± short-acting opioid, with a dedicated airway operator. In peri-arrest, shock first.
  • Pad position: switch anterior–posterior if anterolateral fails; it improves the current vector through the atria.
  • If it fails: the AHA algorithm names three moves — treat the underlying cause, increase the energy for the next attempt, and add an antiarrhythmic before re-shocking (which raises the myocardium's responsiveness). And get expert consultation.

When cardioversion keeps failing or the rhythm keeps recurring

ProblemThink aboutDo
Converts, then immediately re-initiatesOngoing trigger — catecholamines, ectopy, ischemia, hypoxia, electrolytes, pain, stimulant dripsLoad an antiarrhythmic before the next shock. Correct K⁺/Mg²⁺. Reduce β-agonist infusions. Treat pain and agitation. Reassess for ischemia and PE.
Will not convert at allIs this actually a re-entrant rhythm? Automatic rhythms (focal AT, MAT, junctional ectopic, sinus) cannot be cardiovertedRe-read the ECG. If automatic, stop shocking and treat the cause and the rate.
Incessant tachycardia with a falling EFTachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy developing in real timeUrgent EP consultation for ablation — sometimes performed while critically ill, because the arrhythmia is the disease.
Refractory despite everythingOverdrive pacing (atrial pacing above the tachycardia rate can entrain and terminate re-entrant SVT and flutter); rarely AV nodal ablation with pacingElectrophysiology. In post-cardiac-surgery patients, epicardial atrial wires are often already in place and make overdrive pacing straightforward.
Post-conversion pauses or bradycardiaUnderlying sick sinus syndrome unmasked (tachy-brady)Have transcutaneous pacing ready; consider temporary transvenous pacing before further nodal blockade. This patient may need a permanent pacemaker before they can take rate-control drugs.

Special ICU populations

PopulationWhat is different
Post-cardiac surgeryJunctional ectopic tachycardia and atrial arrhythmias are common. Epicardial pacing wires allow overdrive pacing and atrial electrograms — the single best diagnostic tool available for an unclear rhythm. Treat pain, correct Mg²⁺ and K⁺, and look for tamponade.
Heart transplantThe denervated heart is supersensitive to adenosine — prolonged asystole has been reported. Reduce the dose drastically or avoid entirely; have pacing immediately available. Vagal maneuvers do not work on a denervated heart.
Severe COPD / asthma on the ventilatorMAT is the typical rhythm and reflects the severity of the lung disease. Fix oxygenation, ventilation and acidosis; reduce β-agonist and theophylline load. Avoid beta-blockers; verapamil/diltiazem and magnesium are preferred. Do not cardiovert MAT.
Septic shockSinus tachycardia is compensation — treat the sepsis. If a genuine SVT is present and compromising output, esmolol is the most controllable option, but be certain the rhythm is not sinus before removing the compensation.
Thyroid stormBeta-blockers are therapeutic for both the arrhythmia and the storm. Treat the thyroid aggressively — the rhythm will not settle otherwise.
Digoxin toxicityClassically causes atrial tachycardia with block and junctional tachycardia. Check the level and potassium; give digoxin-specific Fab fragments when indicated. Avoid cardioversion where possible — it can precipitate refractory ventricular arrhythmia in the digoxin-toxic myocardium.
PregnancyAdenosine is safe in all trimesters; cardioversion is safe at all stages with fetal monitoring and left lateral tilt. Metoprolol preferred if a beta-blocker is needed; avoid atenolol.
A defibrillator/monitor/pacer. Before any elective cardioversion: pads on, SYNC confirmed with visible R-wave markers, sedation ready, airway equipment and a dedicated airway operator, and suction working.

Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor — with the "not yet" list

Ready for the floor when all are true:
  • Sinus rhythm sustained ≥6–12 hours with no recurrence requiring intervention
  • Off all antiarrhythmic infusions for ≥6 hours, transitioned to oral therapy and tolerating it
  • Off vasopressors ≥6 hours with SBP >100 mmHg and MAP >65 without support
  • No cardioversion in the preceding 24 hours
  • Lactate normalised, urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h, mentation at baseline
  • QTc <500 ms and QRS not widened >25% over baseline on the current regimen
  • K⁺ >4.0 and Mg²⁺ >2.0, stable on the current repletion plan
  • Not requiring NIV or supplemental oxygen beyond the floor's capability
  • A definitive plan exists — ablation scheduled, or the reversible cause identified and treated
Not yet, even if the numbers look fine, if: the rhythm is pre-excited AF and the pathway has not yet been addressed · a wide-complex tachycardia remains unexplained · the patient is within 24 h of starting sotalol, dofetilide or ibutilide and still needs QTc surveillance · there were post-conversion pauses >3 s and pacing capability is still needed · the EF is newly and significantly reduced without an echo plan · or the arrhythmia has recurred more than once during this admission without a definitive plan in place. "Stable at the moment" is not the same as "stable."

ICU disposition beyond the floor: most patients step down and then go home. Consider palliative care involvement when recurrent SVT is one more burden in advanced illness and repeated cardioversions no longer serve the patient's goals; consider LTAC only when a prolonged critical illness — not the arrhythmia — has created ventilator or complex-wound dependence.

Pearls

Practice-changing pearls

💡

The things that separate a good SVT plan from a dangerous one

  1. Get the ECG before you convert them. The tracing during tachycardia is the single most valuable piece of data in the entire encounter, and it is unrecoverable once you push adenosine. If the patient is stable enough to talk to you, they are stable enough for a 12-lead.
  2. A regular narrow tachycardia at almost exactly 150 bpm is atrial flutter with 2:1 block until you prove otherwise. The atrial rate in typical flutter is ~300; halve it and you get the number that fools everyone. Look for sawtooth in II, III, aVF and V1 — and if you cannot see it, that is exactly what adenosine is for.
  3. Irregular + wide + fast = pre-excited AF. No AV-nodal blockers. Adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers and digoxin can all convert this into ventricular fibrillation. Give procainamide or electricity. And note that ESC 2019 also rates IV amiodarone Class III here — older teaching that amiodarone is a safe fallback is out of date.
  4. Adenosine failures are usually technique failures. Half-life under 10 seconds. Large proximal vein, stopcock with a 20 mL flush pushed back-to-back, arm elevated, rhythm strip running. A "non-responder" through a hand vein has usually never received a therapeutic dose.
  5. Halve the adenosine dose for a central line, dipyridamole, or carbamazepine — and think hard before giving it at all to a transplanted heart. Denervation supersensitivity can produce prolonged asystole. Conversely, patients on theophylline or heavy caffeine are competitively antagonised and may need more.
  6. The modified Valsalva is a real intervention, not a formality. REVERT: 43% versus 17% conversion, NNT ≈ 4, no serious adverse events. The postural component — flat plus 15 seconds of passive leg raise immediately after the strain — is the trial. Teach it to the patient before discharge; it is a therapy they take home.
  7. Termination of the tachycardia with a P wave after the last QRS argues against atrial tachycardia. If the rhythm stops on a blocked P, the atrium was still firing and the node was the limiting step — which is inconsistent with an atrial focus driving the rhythm.
  8. A troponin bump after SVT is usually demand ischemia through normal coronaries — reported in roughly 15–50% of cases, with no demonstrated effect on 30- or 90-day mortality. Do not reflexively activate the cath lab. Equally, do not dismiss it in a patient with genuine risk factors and ongoing pain. Trend it and let the whole picture decide.
  9. T-wave inversions after conversion are cardiac memory, not ischemia. They follow a period of abnormal ventricular activation and can persist for days to weeks. Recognising this prevents a great deal of unnecessary testing.
  10. Ask about polyuria and neck pounding. Post-episode polyuria reflects atrial-stretch ANP release; visible regular cannon A waves ("frog sign") reflect atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve and point specifically at AVNRT (~51% in typical AVNRT). Two questions, high yield, zero cost.
  11. Onset and offset are diagnostic. Instant on, instant off = re-entry. Gradual warm-up and cool-down = automatic focus or sinus tachycardia. This distinction from the history often outperforms the ECG you eventually obtain.
  12. SVT is frequently misdiagnosed as panic disorder for years. The discriminator: in SVT the palpitations come first and the anxiety follows; in panic the anxiety builds first and the rate ramps gradually. Ask which came first — and believe the answer.
  13. Ablation is safer than the drugs and it is curative. 97% acute success for AVNRT with 2% recurrence and a 0.3% complication rate. Offer it early rather than committing a 25-year-old to decades of a beta-blocker; many patients accept on the second or third conversation.
  14. Abrupt loss of the delta wave on exercise means a low-risk pathway. Gradual fading does not. This distinction is frequently misread and it changes whether the patient needs an EP study.
  15. Never cardiovert MAT. There is no single circuit to break. Fix the lungs, correct the gases, reduce β-agonists, give magnesium.
  16. In the ICU, wide-complex means VT until proven otherwise. Roughly 80% of undifferentiated wide-complex tachycardia is VT, over 90% with prior MI, and age >35 alone gives a PPV near 85%. Brugada and Vereckei shift the probability; they do not give you permission to treat it as SVT.
  17. Phenylephrine is the thinking pressor in tachyarrhythmic shock. Pure α₁ raises pressure without adding β-stimulation to a heart you are trying to slow, and the reflex vagal response can help terminate the SVT. Every β-agonist you hang works against your antiarrhythmic.
  18. Ask "is this rhythm the problem, or the response to the problem?" Sinus tachycardia and MAT are responses — rate-controlling them removes the patient's compensation. AVNRT and AVRT are problems. This single question prevents the most consequential errors on this page.
  19. Etripamil (CARDAMYST) changed the outpatient conversation in 2025. Self-administered nasal spray, 70 mg with one repeat at 10 minutes, 64% conversion by 30 minutes versus 31% placebo. It gives patients who decline ablation a way to abort episodes at home — and, tellingly, it is contraindicated in pre-excitation for exactly the reasons above.
  20. Check a TSH, and check a pregnancy test. One finds a reversible cause you will otherwise chase for months; the other rewrites the entire drug list and the fluoroscopy plan.
  21. Several familiar habits are now out of date — audit yours. Cardioversion energies changed in 2025 (narrow-complex 100 J, AF and flutter 200 J; low-energy shocks are explicitly discouraged). ESC 2019 deleted amiodarone and digoxin from acute narrow-complex management, removed sotalol and lidocaine from acute wide-complex management with the key message "do not use sotalol in patients with SVT," and replaced verapamil/diltiazem and ablation for inappropriate sinus tachycardia with ivabradine ± a beta-blocker. If your practice still reflects the older versions, it is worth updating deliberately rather than by accident.
  22. Where the two big guidelines disagree, say so out loud. Adenosine escalation: ESC 2019 goes 6 → 12 → 18 mg, while AHA ACLS and the US label stop at 6 → 12 mg. Sotalol: Class IIb for ACC/AHA/HRS 2015, "do not use" for ESC 2019. Knowing that a disagreement exists — rather than half-remembering one side — is what lets you defend your choice on rounds.

Refs

Sources, trials & media

Guidelines & primary sources

  • 2019 ESC Guidelines for the management of patients with supraventricular tachycardia — Brugada J, Katritsis DG, et al. Eur Heart J 2020;41:655–720 · ESC guideline page. Primary anchor for this guide — epidemiology (prevalence 2.25/1000; incidence 35/100,000 person-years), ablation success/complication rates (Table 11), IV drug doses, the diltiazem 120 mg + propranolol 80 mg pill-in-the-pocket regimen, and the Class III rating for IV amiodarone in pre-excited AF.
  • 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Management of Adult Patients With Supraventricular Tachycardia — Page RL, et al. Circulation 2016;133:e506–e574 · JACC.
  • 2025 AHA Adult Tachyarrhythmia With a Pulse Algorithm — American Heart Association (PDF). Source for the instability criteria, the adenosine 6 → 12 mg sequence, and the procainamide and amiodarone infusion doses.
  • 2025 AHA Electrical Cardioversion Algorithm — American Heart Association (PDF). Source for the current energies: narrow-complex 100 J, atrial flutter 200 J, atrial fibrillation 200 J, monomorphic VT 100 J, polymorphic VT unsynchronized defibrillation — superseding the legacy 50–100 J teaching. Also the bedside-preparation and sedation notes. Corresponding 2025 AHA Part 9 statements: AF ≥200 J initial (COR 2a, LOE B-R); flutter 200 J initial (COR 2b, LOE C-LD).
  • CARDAMYST (etripamil) nasal spray — FDA label: DailyMed · FDA (PDF). 70 mg initial, repeat 70 mg after 10 min, max 140 mg/24 h; contraindicated in WPW/pre-excitation, NYHA II–IV HF, sick sinus without pacemaker, Mobitz II or higher block.
  • USPSTF recommendations: Hypertension (A) · Tobacco (A) · Alcohol (B) · Statins (B) · Diabetes (B).
  • StatPearls — Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia: NCBI Bookshelf. AAFP review (2023): Common Types of Supraventricular Tachycardia — chronic oral dose ranges.
  • LITFL ECG Library — VT versus SVT: litfl.com. Brugada morphology criteria and features favouring VT.

Key trials & landmark studies

Trial / studyYearResultWhy it matters
REVERT2015Modified (postural) Valsalva vs standard: sinus restored in 93/214 (43%) vs 37/214 (17%); no serious adverse eventsMade the leg-raise modification standard of care. NNT ≈ 4 for a free, zero-risk intervention that can be taught to the patient.
RAPID (etripamil)202364% vs 31% conversion within 30 min; median time to conversion 17 vs 54 min; 74% vs 56% at 60 minPhase 3 trial behind the 2025 FDA approval of CARDAMYST — the first self-administered, at-home abortive therapy for PSVT.
NODE-3012022Etripamil 70 mg: 53.7% vs 34.7% conversion at 30 minFirst randomised placebo-controlled study of self-administered intranasal etripamil for spontaneous PSVT.
NODE-3032024Open-label safety: adverse events predominantly local and mild (68%) to moderate (31%); no serious etripamil-related eventsEstablished the real-world safety profile supporting unsupervised patient self-administration.
Brugada criteria1991554 wide-complex tachycardias; stepwise algorithm with sensitivity 98.7%, specificity 96.5% in derivationThe reference algorithm for VT vs SVT with aberrancy. Independent validation is far weaker (sens ~89%, spec ~59%) — know both numbers.
Vereckei aVR algorithm2008483 tachycardias; sensitivity 96.5%, specificity 95.7% using lead aVR aloneSimplified single-lead approach; superior overall accuracy to Brugada in the original comparison, but real-world specificity by non-specialists is much lower.
Vereckei (EHJ)2007NPV for VT 83.5% vs 65.2% for Brugada; superior overall accuracy (P = 0.006)Introduced the vi/vt ventricular activation velocity ratio concept.
ESC Table 11 registry synthesis2019Ablation: AVNRT 97%/2%/0.3%, AVRT 92%/8%/1.5%, focal AT 85%/20%/1.4%, CTI flutter 95%/10%/2% (success/recurrence/complications)The numbers you quote when consenting a patient for ablation.
PROCAMIO2017IV procainamide vs amiodarone for stable wide-QRS tachycardia: fewer major cardiac adverse events and better tachycardia termination with procainamideCited in ESC 2019; underpins procainamide's preference over amiodarone for stable wide-complex tachycardia.
CAST1989–91Class IC antiarrhythmics after MI increased mortalityThe reason flecainide and propafenone require a structurally normal heart and a clean echo before prescribing.

Educational reference for an incoming IM resident. Every dose and threshold on this page is traceable to the sources listed above — verify against your institution's formulary and the current guideline before acting on any individual patient. Class-of-recommendation labels are quoted only where the source guideline states them explicitly; where a criterion is given without a class label, none was verifiable. Where a published frequency does not exist, this guide says so rather than estimating.
